findings.title: Jupyter kernel HMAC verification is a no-op stub; all inbound messages accepted
findings.description: verify_message() returns Ok(()) unconditionally: after the key-empty early return it computes frames_for_signing() then discards them with 'let _ = frames;' and returns Ok(()) without ever calling hmac::verify. The on-wire hmac_hex frame is discarded by parse_message() (lines 271-312) so it is not even available. The working verifier verify_message_with_signature() is marked #[allow(dead_code)] (line 338) and never invoked. Main loop line 225 calls the stub, so unsigned/forged execute_request messages are compiled and executed (rustc spawn + binary execution), violating the Jupyter spec requirement that unverified messages be dropped.
findings.root_cause: parse_message() drops the signature frame and verify_message() was left as an unimplemented stub; the correct verifier exists but was never wired into the dispatch loop.
findings.impact: Any local process can send execute_request to the kernel's shell socket and run arbitrary Buff code (full rustc compile + native execution) without the shared key. If the kernel is bound non-loopback (see AUD-SEC-002) this becomes unauthenticated remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: Retain hmac_hex in WireMessage, call hmac::verify(key, frames, sig) in verify_message for every shell and control message, remove #[allow(dead_code)] from verify_message_with_signature, and add an integration test asserting unsigned messages are dropped when a key is configured.
fix_guide: Add signature_hex field to WireMessage; capture post[1] (hmac frame index) in parse_message instead of discarding it.
Change verify_message to take the signature and delegate to hmac::verify; call it for both shell and control dispatch paths.
Delete the #[allow(dead_code)] variant or make it the single implementation; add a test that a message with wrong signature is dropped when key is non-empty.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 60 min wire-format change + 30 min loop wiring + 30 min tests

findings.technology: Rust, zeromq, hmac-sha256, Jupyter kernel protocol v5

confidence.rationale: Stub body read directly: computes frames then 'let _ = frames; Ok(())'; dead-code attribute on the real verifier confirmed at line 338; loop call site at line 225 confirmed.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: Code comments themselves admit real verification is not wired ('requires the raw multipart which is not retained here'). No interpretation needed.
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: No convention legitimizes skipping HMAC; AGENTS.md states 'HMAC-SHA256 auth' as shipped behavior, making this an implementation gap, not a documented choice.

findings.title: Kernel binds sockets to arbitrary connection-file IP; no loopback restriction or warning
findings.description: ConnectionFile::validate() only checks transport=='tcp' and signature_scheme; the ip field is never validated and the field doc (line 44) explicitly blesses '*' and '0.0.0.0'. ZmqSocketSet::bind (transport.rs:123-153) binds shell/iopub/control/hb sockets to exactly that endpoint. A connection file with ip='0.0.0.0' exposes an execute-capable kernel to the network with no warning. Combined with AUD-SEC-001 (HMAC never enforced) this yields unauthenticated remote code execution; even with HMAC fixed, unsigned mode (empty key+scheme) is also accepted by validate() (test line 219-233).
findings.root_cause: validate() scope limited to transport/scheme enumeration; no policy check on the bind address and no warning when key is empty.
findings.impact: One config line (or a default in a container/remote-kernel setup) turns a local dev kernel into a network-reachable code-execution service; Jupyter's own tooling warns in this scenario, this kernel does not.
findings.recommendation: In validate() reject or warn on non-loopback ip unless an explicit opt-in env var (e.g. BUFF_JUPYTER_ALLOW_REMOTE=1) is set; refuse empty signature_scheme+key unless the same opt-in is present; print the bind address and auth mode at startup.
fix_guide: Add loopback check for ip in ConnectionFile::validate with env-var override for intentional remote use.
Emit a loud warning when key/signature_scheme are empty.
Add unit tests for 0.0.0.0/* rejection and override acceptance.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 30 min validation + 15 min warning + 15 min tests

findings.verification_command: Select-String -Path crates/buff-jupyter/src/connection.rs -Pattern 'pub fn validate' -Context 0,15; Select-String -Path crates/buff-jupyter/src/connection.rs -Pattern '0\.0\.0\.0'

confidence.rationale: Validation code and doc comments read directly; exploitability of the bind alone is capped because AUD-SEC-001 is the true enabler, hence medium not high.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: The 0.0.0.0 acceptance is documented in the field comment, but documentation is not an opt-in security control; the gap is a missing guard, not a claimed feature.
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: No convention addresses remote binds; T129a scope notes tcp-only, silent on ip policy.

findings.title: buffup verifies downloads with checksum from the same origin as the artifact (no signature)
findings.description: fetch_checksum_sidecar() downloads '<tarball_url>.sha256' from the same GitHub host serving the tarball (line 122: format!("{tarball_url}.sha256")); install.rs:78-84 compares SHA-256. This defends against corruption only: any adversary able to substitute the tarball (compromised release workflow, GitHub account, malicious redirect of both URLs) can equally substitute the sidecar. The installed artifact is an executable placed on PATH, so the trust requirement is integrity against an active adversary, which requires an independent signing key (rustup uses GPG; Homebrew uses its own seal). --skip-checksum is documented and warned, so the flag itself is not a finding.
findings.root_cause: P0.9 hardening added integrity verification but no out-of-band trust anchor; sidecar trust equals artifact trust by construction.
findings.impact: A supply-chain compromise of the release channel defeats the only download-integrity control; users executing `buffup install` would run attacker-controlled binaries with the checksum reporting OK.
findings.recommendation: Publish a detached minisign/sigstore signature made by a long-lived key whose public half ships in buffup (or is pinned via a separate channel); verify the signature (not just the hash) before unpack; keep the sha256 check as a fast-fail.
fix_guide: Add release workflow step producing a minisign/sigstore signature over the tarball.
Embed the verifying public key in the buffup binary; fetch and verify signature before extract.
Document the trust model in crates/buffup/README.md.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 120 min workflow + 90 min verify impl + 60 min tests/docs; workflow changes need release-infra coordination

findings.technology: Rust, reqwest (rustls), sha2, minisign/sigstore, GitHub Releases

confidence.rationale: Code path read directly; the weakness is architectural (same-origin sidecar) and certain, but severity is medium because exploitation requires compromising the HTTPS/GitHub release channel.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: The check exists and is commented as a supply-chain mitigation (install.rs:69-70); the finding is that the mitigation's trust anchor is circular, not that code is missing.
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: Not a documented deliberate acceptance; P0.9 labels it a 'supply chain attack mitigation', which same-origin hashing does not deliver.

findings.title: Registry bearer and session tokens stored unhashed at rest in SQLite
findings.description: add_token() inserts the raw bearer token ('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tokens (token) VALUES (?1)', line 211) and session creation stores raw session tokens in the sessions table (line 572). validate_token() then compares by SQL string equality (lines 396-408); InMemoryStorage uses HashSet::contains (storage.rs:587-593). Any read of registry.db (backup leak, path traversal elsewhere, incident response artifact) yields live publish credentials. crates.io stores only SHA-256 digests of tokens for exactly this reason. The non-constant-time comparison is low practical risk (network timing over SQL/B-tree and Rust's SipHash seeding) and is noted, not the core issue.
findings.root_cause: Tokens treated as lookups-by-equality rather than secrets-at-rest; no digest-at-rest design in the T57 storage layer.
findings.impact: Database-file compromise converts directly into account/publish takeover with no cracking step; revocation forensics are harder since plaintext tokens can be re-inserted.
findings.recommendation: Store SHA-256(token) (or HMAC with a server pepper) in tokens/sessions tables; compare digests on validation; migrate with a one-time rehash prompt for existing rows.

fix_examples.before: conn.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tokens (token) VALUES (?1)", params![token])

fix_guide: Add token_hash column; write digest on add_token and session create.
Provide a migration that drops or rehashes legacy plaintext rows; document in crate docs.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 60 min schema + 60 min call sites + 60 min migration/tests

findings.verification_command: Select-String -Path crates/buff-registry/src/storage_sqlite.rs -Pattern 'INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tokens|INSERT INTO sessions|fn validate_token' | Select-Object LineNumber, Line

confidence.rationale: Insert statements and validators read directly in source; plaintext at rest is factual, severity low because the DB is loopback-bound and typically local.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: MVP crates may accept short-term tradeoffs, but no doc declares plaintext-at-rest a deliberate choice; AGENTS.md says 'in-memory storage' while SQLite persistence shipped silently into the same design.
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: crates/buff-registry/AGENTS.md lists SQLite backend; no hashing requirement stated either way.

findings.title: buff login writes ~/.buff/credentials without restrictive permissions
findings.description: save_credentials_to() creates parent dirs and writes the TOML containing the bearer token with plain fs::write (line 238). On Unix with default umask 022 the file lands 0644, readable by every local user on shared/CI hosts; no 0600 chmod (Unix) or restrictive ACL (Windows) is applied, unlike `cargo login` which sets 0600. The doc comment only acknowledges missing atomic write ('temp-file + rename' future hardening, line 224) and is silent on permissions, so this is not a documented acceptance.
findings.root_cause: Plain fs::write used for a secret-bearing file without post-write permission tightening.
findings.impact: On multi-user Unix systems any local account can read the registry token and publish packages impersonating the victim.
findings.recommendation: After write, set mode 0600 on Unix via std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt (and pre-create with OpenOptions mode 0o600); on Windows note that profile-dir ACLs apply, or set an owner-only ACL; write via temp file + rename for atomicity at the same time.

fix_examples.before:
fs::write(path, text)
    .with_context(|| format!("failed to write credentials to {}", path.display()))?;

fix_guide: Apply 0600 via PermissionsExt on unix after write (cfg-gated).
Optionally create via OpenOptionsExt::mode(0o600) to avoid a window at 0644.
Add a test asserting the mode on unix targets.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 20 min impl + 15 min test + 10 min docs

confidence.rationale: Function body read in full; no permission call exists anywhere in the file (grep for PermissionsExt/0o600 returned only the two function definitions).

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: Windows-local development makes this invisible day-to-day, but the code path is cross-platform and the omission is objective; low severity chosen because exploitation requires a shared multi-user host.
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: No convention covers credential-file modes; doc comment covers atomicity only, so permissions were overlooked rather than declined.

findings.title: Publish endpoints store dependency names without validation, bypassing the P0.28 layered defense
findings.description: Both publish (request.deps used at line 418 has_cycle and stored at lines 447-455) and multipart_publish (meta.deps stored at lines 820-829) accept DepSpec.name strings with no validate_no_path_traversal/validate_package_name call, even though the P0.28 header (lines 56-65) states the traversal guard 'runs on EVERY user-supplied path-y input'. A dep name like '../evil' or '@org/pkg/extra' is persisted and later echoed in package metadata and walked by has_cycle. Today dep names never reach the filesystem (tarball paths use validated name+version), so there is no direct exploit; this is a defense-in-depth gap against the crate's own stated invariant and future storage backends that might key on dep names.
findings.root_cause: Validation added per-field at handler doors (name, version) but the nested deps array was missed when P0.28 layered the three checks.
findings.impact: Persisted unvalidated strings expand the stored-attack-payload surface and silently violate the documented 'every path-y input' guarantee; a future backend (SqliteStorage already persists deps JSON) could turn these into query/path keys.
findings.recommendation: Validate every DepSpec.name in both publish paths with validate_no_path_traversal + validate_package_name (dep names follow the same package-name grammar), returning 400 InvalidInput on failure.
fix_guide: Add a validate_deps(&[DepSpec]) helper calling the existing validators per entry.
Call it in publish and multipart_publish before has_cycle/put_version.
Add unit tests for '../evil', 'a/b/c', and '@org/pkg' dep names.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 20 min helper + 20 min wiring both handlers + 20 min tests

findings.verification_command: Select-String -Path crates/buff-registry/src/handlers.rs -Pattern 'deps' | Select-Object LineNumber, Line; Select-String -Path crates/buff-registry/src/handlers.rs -Pattern 'validate_no_path_traversal|validate_package_name' | Select-Object LineNumber, Line

confidence.rationale: All publish-path lines inspected; no validator call site touches deps. Severity capped at low because current storage never uses dep names as paths or query params.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: The gap is real but latent; the crate's own comment establishes the violated invariant, making this a policy-vs-implementation mismatch rather than taste.
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: P0.28 section in handlers.rs (lines 50-75) is the governing convention; AGENTS.md documents validation as a handler concern.
